passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uncomfortable position within Anglo-American contract law, for it permits courts to enforce promises that would otherwise fail for want of consideration — the traditional prerequisite for a legally binding agreement. Under classical contract doctrine, a promise is enforceable only if the promisee has provided something of value in exchange; without that exchange, a gratuitous promise, however sincerely made and however much the promisee has relied upon it, is ordinarily not cognizable in law. Promissory estoppel challenges this orthodoxy by holding that, where a promisor ought reasonably to have foreseen that his promise would induce the promisee to act in substantial and definite ways, and where such reliance has in fact occurred, justice may require enforcement even in the absence of consideration.

American courts have applied this doctrine with notably inconsistent results, and the source of that inconsistency can be located in a single ambiguity: whether the remedy awarded upon a successful promissory-estoppel claim should be measured by the promisee's expectation interest — placing the promisee in the position he would have occupied had the promise been performed — or only by the promisee's reliance interest — restoring the promisee to the position he occupied before the promise was made. In a 1987 case decided by a federal appellate court in the Seventh Circuit, a supplier who had prepared extensive tooling and inventory in reliance on a manufacturer's oral assurance of a long-term supply contract was awarded expectation damages, on the ground that anything less would inadequately vindicate the supplier's reasonable reliance. Yet in a 1993 decision by a state appellate court in the same region, a contractor who had restructured his workforce on the strength of an analogous assurance received only reliance damages, the court reasoning that promissory estoppel should not be permitted to collapse into ordinary contract liability. These two rulings rest on incompatible premises about the doctrine's purpose.

The deeper difficulty is that courts have never settled whether promissory estoppel is a freestanding cause of action or merely an equitable doctrine invoked to prevent unjust enrichment. If the former, it arguably demands full expectation damages; if the latter, restoration of the status quo ante may suffice. This ambiguity has allowed courts to reach pragmatically convenient outcomes without committing to any principled account of the doctrine's foundations. The consequence is a body of case law that affords contracting parties inadequate guidance and that threatens to make every informal commercial assurance a source of potential liability of indeterminate magnitude. Courts would do well to resolve this foundational question explicitly rather than continuing to finesse it on a case-by-case basis — a practice that, however understandable as a judicial management strategy, ultimately disserves both commercial certainty and the interests of relying parties.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be abolished because it undermines the classical requirement of consideration in contract law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: American courts have applied the doctrine of promissory estoppel inconsistently because they have not resolved whether the doctrine is an independent cause of action or merely an equitable remedy, and this unresolved ambiguity harms contracting parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 1987 and 1993 appellate decisions illustrate that federal and state courts apply different standards of damages in contract disputes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should always award expectation damages rather than reliance damages in order to fully vindicate the promisee's reasonable reliance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel provides contracting parties with adequate guidance about the circumstances under which an informal assurance becomes legally binding.

explanations.correct: The passage traces inconsistent application (paragraphs 2–3) to a foundational ambiguity about promissory estoppel's nature (paragraph 3) and closes by arguing this ambiguity disserves contracting parties. B integrates both strands.
explanations.A: The author does not advocate abolition; the closing prescription is for courts to resolve the foundational question, not to eliminate the doctrine.
explanations.C: Too narrow — the two cases are illustrative examples of the broader inconsistency problem, not the passage's main point. The passage is not primarily about federal-versus-state court differences.
explanations.D: The author withholds judgment on which damages measure is correct; the prescription is only that courts should resolve the question explicitly, not that one answer is right.
explanations.E: This directly contradicts the passage's claim that the case law leaves contracting parties without adequate guidance.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, under classical contract doctrine a promise is enforceable only if

choices.label: A
choices.text: the promisee has acted in substantial reliance upon it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the promisor could reasonably have foreseen the promisee's reliance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the promisee has provided something of value in exchange.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the promise is made in writing and witnessed by a third party.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the agreement has been reviewed by a court of equity.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 states explicitly: 'a promise is enforceable only if the promisee has provided something of value in exchange.' C is a direct paraphrase.
explanations.A: This describes the promissory-estoppel standard, not the classical consideration requirement.
explanations.B: Reasonable foreseeability of reliance is the promissory-estoppel standard articulated later in paragraph 1, not the classical rule.
explanations.D: The passage never mentions written form or witnessing as requirements of classical contract doctrine.
explanations.E: The passage does not state that equity court review is a prerequisite under classical doctrine.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that in the 1993 state appellate decision, the contractor received only reliance damages because the court

choices.label: A
choices.text: found that the contractor had not incurred substantial costs in reliance on the manufacturer's assurance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: concluded that promissory estoppel should not be allowed to collapse into ordinary contract liability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: determined that the oral assurance did not satisfy the requirements for promissory estoppel.

choices.label: D
choices.text: held that expectation damages were unavailable because the parties had never agreed on a contract price.

choices.label: E
choices.text: reasoned that the contractor's reliance was not foreseeable to the manufacturer at the time the assurance was made.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states: 'the court reasoning that promissory estoppel should not be permitted to collapse into ordinary contract liability.' B is a close paraphrase.
explanations.A: The passage does not indicate that the contractor's reliance was found insubstantial; the contractor did restructure his workforce.
explanations.C: The court awarded reliance damages, implying the promissory-estoppel claim succeeded; the dispute was about the remedy, not the doctrine's applicability.
explanations.D: The passage does not mention any disagreement about contract price as the reason for the damages limitation.
explanations.E: Foreseeability of reliance is not given as the 1993 court's rationale; the issue was the appropriate remedy.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts that award expectation damages in promissory-estoppel cases are more faithful to the doctrine's equitable origins than courts that award only reliance damages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A contracting party who gives an informal oral assurance should, under current doctrine, be able to predict with confidence the financial consequences of that assurance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Until courts articulate a coherent account of promissory estoppel's foundational purpose, the doctrine will continue to produce unpredictable outcomes for commercial parties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is best understood as an equitable doctrine designed solely to prevent unjust enrichment, and expectation damages are therefore never appropriate.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The inconsistency in promissory-estoppel decisions stems primarily from the different procedural rules governing federal and state appellate courts.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 argues that courts have avoided committing to a principled account, producing indeterminate liability and inadequate guidance. C is a well-hedged inference combining those two points.
explanations.A: The author does not endorse either damages measure as more faithful; the author calls for a resolution, not for one particular answer.
explanations.B: This contradicts the passage's explicit claim that the body of case law 'affords contracting parties inadequate guidance.'
explanations.D: The author presents this as one possible view but does not endorse it; the passage explicitly frames this as an unresolved question.
explanations.E: The passage locates the inconsistency in a doctrinal ambiguity, not in procedural differences between federal and state courts.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the practice of courts resolving promissory-estoppel cases on a case-by-case basis without committing to a foundational principle can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unqualified admiration, because it allows judges to reach equitable outcomes in individual disputes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: cautious approval tempered by concern that the approach may occasionally produce anomalous results.

choices.label: C
choices.text: critical acceptance, acknowledging that it is understandable as a judicial strategy while maintaining that it ultimately disserves important interests.

choices.label: D
choices.text: outright condemnation, with the author urging that all promissory-estoppel claims be transferred to a specialized commercial court.

choices.label: E
choices.text: neutral description, with no evaluative stance expressed.

explanations.correct: The closing sentence explicitly concedes that case-by-case finessing is 'understandable as a judicial management strategy' while immediately qualifying it as one that 'ultimately disserves both commercial certainty and the interests of relying parties.' C captures both the concession and the criticism.
explanations.A: The author does not admire this practice; the passage ends with a prescription to abandon it.
explanations.B: 'Cautious approval' misreads the author's stance, which is predominantly critical despite the concession.
explanations.D: 'Outright condemnation' overstates the tone, and no specialized court is mentioned; the author calls for explicit resolution, not institutional transfer.
explanations.E: The author clearly evaluates the practice negatively, so the characterization as neutral is inaccurate.

questions.questionStem: The author most likely discusses the 1987 Seventh Circuit decision and the 1993 state appellate decision in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that federal appellate courts consistently award more generous damages than state appellate courts in contract disputes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate, through two contrasting outcomes, that the ambiguity about the proper remedy in promissory-estoppel cases has produced incompatible rulings.

choices.label: C
choices.text: argue that the Seventh Circuit's reasoning in 1987 was legally superior to the state court's reasoning in 1993.

choices.label: D
choices.text: provide a historical account of how promissory estoppel evolved from an equitable doctrine into a freestanding cause of action.

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that oral assurances made by manufacturers are more legally risky than those made by contractors.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 explicitly says 'These two rulings rest on incompatible premises about the doctrine's purpose.' The cases are introduced to illustrate the inconsistency that the passage has already identified as the central problem. B captures this rhetorical function.
explanations.A: The passage does not advance a general claim about federal versus state generosity in damages; the two cases involve different parties and factual settings, and the author does not endorse this generalization.
explanations.C: The author explicitly refrains from endorsing either result; the point is that the two rulings are incompatible, not that one is superior.
explanations.D: The cases are not presented as historical waypoints in the doctrine's evolution; the passage is concerned with their incompatible premises about remedies.
explanations.E: The passage draws no such comparison about the legal risk of assurances by manufacturers versus contractors.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and its classical antecedents traced; two conflicting applications of the doctrine are presented; the deeper ambiguity underlying those conflicts is identified and a resolution is prescribed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and defined; a single paradigm case illustrating its correct application is analyzed in detail; a recommendation for legislative reform is advanced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrinal controversy is described; two scholarly positions on the controversy are summarized and compared; the author endorses one position as clearly superior.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The history of a common-law rule is traced from its origins to the present day; recent judicial departures from the rule are criticized; a return to the original formulation is urged.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A doctrine's definition is provided; its inconsistent application across jurisdictions is attributed to poor judicial draftsmanship; several specific drafting improvements are proposed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel and contrasts it with classical consideration doctrine. Paragraph 2 presents the two conflicting cases. Paragraph 3 locates the deeper foundational ambiguity and closes with a prescription for courts to resolve it. A tracks all three moves accurately.
explanations.B: The passage discusses two cases, not one paradigm case; and the closing prescription is directed at courts, not the legislature.
explanations.C: The passage does not summarize two scholarly positions; the conflicting approaches are judicial, and the author does not endorse either damages measure as clearly superior.
explanations.D: The passage does not trace a historical evolution of the rule, and does not urge return to an original formulation; it urges a principled resolution of an existing ambiguity.
explanations.E: The passage attributes inconsistency to a foundational doctrinal ambiguity, not to poor draftsmanship, and proposes no specific drafting fixes.
